upperLimit.source: No UL set: ICMR-NIN TUL not found; NASEM 1998, EFSA and UK EVM 2003 set none. App notice uses the UK guidance level of 40 mg/day from supplements (Food Standards Scotland), which is not a formal UL

topFoodSources.food: Curd (dahi), est. from IFCT cow milk

absorptionBoosters: whole pulses instead of only split dals
green leafy vegetables such as amaranth, methi and drumstick leaves
storing milk and curd in the dark (fridge, opaque or steel containers)
pressure cooking pulses in measured water and using the cooking water
spreading intake through the day rather than one large dose
absorptionBlockers: sunlight or bright light on milk and curd in clear bottles or pouches
boiling vegetables in excess water and discarding it
cooking rice in excess water and draining it
some medicines (phenothiazine antipsychotics, tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates, probenecid)
warnings: No formal upper limit is set for riboflavin; UK guidance considers up to 40 mg per day from supplements unlikely to cause harm.
Bright yellow urine after B-complex or riboflavin supplements is expected and harmless.
Check labels for duplicate B-complex products; these also contain vitamin B6 and niacin, which matter more for safety.
Milk and curd lose riboflavin quickly in sunlight; store them in the fridge or in opaque containers.
Using riboflavin for migraine should be decided with a doctor.
People who are pregnant or breastfeeding, vegan, on dialysis, drink alcohol heavily or take regular medicines should ask their doctor about B vitamins.
General information, not medical advice. Check with a doctor before starting supplements.
